newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary cenbank says no to rate decline - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Hungary cenbank says no to rate decline - analysts.

text.p: The National Bank of Hungary's (NBH) deposit rate hike on Monday gave the red light to further interest rate decline, so as to prevent a capital outflow from the country, analysts and dealers said.

"Due to the decline of interest rates, the advantages of forint savings were disappearing," said Budapest Bank analyst Peter Bihari. "If they disappear, a capital outflow may begin, so it is a restraint for the NBH to take care of the rates."

The NBH on Monday raised the rate at which it accepts deposits from the commercial banks for six months to 21.00 percent from 20.75, breaking the trend of its almost regular monthly rate cuts in the past few months.
The central bank also launched a 12-month deposit facility at an annual 20.50 percent rate and said in a statement that the moves were aimed at protecting savings.

"Current interest rate levels, or their further decline, do not encourage savings sufficiently, and for the long term they jeopardise further favourable changes in inflation and macroeconomic processes," the NBH said in a statement.

Interbank dealers said the NBH move shocked the markets on which repo cut expectations in the past two weeks substantially reduced liquidity and pushed up interbank rates, encouraging the banks to take advantage of current high NBH repo rates.
"(The hike) hit the market like a bomb," said Commerzbank dealer Sandor Tolonics.

Dealers said that following the NBH moves there were few panic government securities sales, but the yields on government securities, mainly for the six-month and the 12-month maturities, increased slightly and were likely to rise further.
Tolonics said the NBH move indicated its intention to keep forint savings more attractive than foreign currency savings which offer 19 percent yield for one year.
"If forint interest rates are too close to the yields from foreign currency savings, many investors may say that they prefer the greenback," Tolonics said.
Interest rates in Hungary have been dropping almost continuously since the beginning of last year, in line with a 10 percent drop in year-on-year inflation.
Analysts said that following the past few months' interest rate decline, the NBH's concerns over real interest rates were justified, though they did not see signs of a capital outflow yet.
"They (the NBH) are a little bit concerned because perhaps interest rates are coming down a little too quickly," said Nigel Rendell, HSBC James Capel's London-based analyst.
"But I am pretty confident that the overall trend this year is going to be lower rates in Hungary because inflation is improving."
Other analysts said a slowdown in the conversion of foreign currencies into forints was a warning sign.
"There was conversion in January, but in February and March it seemed to halt," Bihari said.

Concorde Securities analyst Peter Muszely said the NBH may have wanted to attract a larger part of the savings in short maturities, as plans for a radical inflation cut for 1998 were serious and believed longer than one year yields were too high.
"They are considering the anti-inflationary programme very strongly," Muszely said.

The government commissioned Finance Minister Peter Medgyessy and central bank president Gyorgy Suranyi to work out a programme for a 1998 inflation cut, which should be larger than the originally planned five percentage points.

Inflation is currently running at 18.8 percent and the NBH expects it to go down to 17 percent by December, while the government and the NBH said they would consider a further cut in the monthly devaluation rate from 1.1 percent in July.
